'''Joanna Dorothy Haigh''' (born 7 May 1954)<ref name=whoswho/> is a British [[physicist]] and academic.<ref name=gs>{{Google scholar id}}</ref><ref>[http://www.open.edu/openlearn/body-mind/ou-on-the-bbc-truth-will-out-global-warming-caused-human-activity Global warming is caused by human activity] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180905044906/http://www.open.edu/openlearn/body-mind/ou-on-the-bbc-truth-will-out-global-warming-caused-human-activity |date=5 September 2018 }} – interview for the [[Open University]]</ref><ref>[https://www.carbonbrief.org/the-carbon-brief-interview-prof-joanna-haigh The Carbon Brief Interview: Prof Joanna Haigh] (29 April 2019)</ref> Before her retirement in 2019<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/191071/climate-champion-jo-haigh-retires-after/|title=Climate champion Jo Haigh retires after 35 years at Imperial {{!}} Imperial News {{!}} Imperial College London|last=Dunning|first=Hayley|website=Imperial News|date=3 May 2019 |language=en|access-date=2019-05-05}}</ref> she was Professor of [[Atmospheric Physics]] at [[Imperial College London]], and co-director of the [[Grantham Institute – Climate Change and Environment]]. She served as head of the Department of Physics at Imperial College London.{{when|date=November 2020}} She is a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS), and served as president of the [[Royal Meteorological Society]].{{when|date=November 2020}}

==Early life and education==
Haigh was born in 1954.<ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | author=Anon| title=Haigh, Prof. Joanna Dorothy | id = U258354 | year = 2014 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U258354|location=Oxford}}</ref> She was educated at [[Hitchin Girls' School]], then an all-girls [[grammar school]] in [[Hitchin]], Hertfordshire. She showed an early interest in the weather, building her own weather station in her back garden as a teenager.<ref name=":0" /> She studied [[physics]] at [[Somerville College, Oxford|Somerville College]], [[University of Oxford|Oxford]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] (BA) degree; as per tradition, this was later promoted to a [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)|Master of Arts]] (Oxon) degree. This was followed by a [[Master of Science]] (MSc) degree in [[meteorology]] at [[Imperial College London]]. She returned to Oxford to complete a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (DPhil) degree in [[atmospheric physics]] under the [[Doctoral supervisor|supervision]] of C.D. Walshaw. This was awarded in 1980 for her [[doctoral thesis]] on ''Experiments with a two-dimensional model of the general circulation''.<ref name="haighphd">{{cite thesis |degree=DPhil |first=Joanna Dorothy|last=Haigh |title=Experiments with a two-dimensional model of the general circulation |publisher=University of Oxford |year=1980 |id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.256537}}|url=https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:e27ea059-59df-4e10-8bb0-050a07ed3957|website=ox.ac.uk|oclc=298511188}} {{free access}}</ref>

==Career and research==
Haigh is [[Emeritus]] Professor of [[atmospheric physics]] at [[Imperial College London]]. She joined [[Imperial College London]] as a lecturer in 1984.<ref name=":0" /> Since 2014, she has served as co-director of the [[Grantham Institute – Climate Change and Environment]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/people/j.haigh|access-date=14 October 2014|title=Home – Professor Joanna D. Haigh}}</ref> She has served as head of the Department of Physics at Imperial College from 2009 to 2014.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/physics/about/historyofphysicsdept/pastheads|access-date=14 October 2014|title=Past Heads of Department}}</ref>

Haigh is known for her work on [[solar variation|solar variability]], and also works on radiative transfer, [[stratosphere]]-[[troposphere]] coupling and [[climate model]]ling.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haigh |first1=J. D. |last2=Roscoe |first2=H. K. |doi=10.1175/2009JCLI2865.1 |title=The Final Warming Date of the Antarctic Polar Vortex and Influences on its Interannual Variability |journal =[[Journal of Climate]] |volume=22 |issue=22 |pages=5809 |year=2009 |bibcode=2009JCli...22.5809H |s2cid=128778821 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/896235 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Haigh | first1 = J. D. | last2 = Blackburn | first2 = M. | doi = 10.1007/s11214-006-9067-0 | title = Solar Influences on Dynamical Coupling Between the Stratosphere and Troposphere | journal = Space Science Reviews | volume = 125 | pages = 331 | year = 2006 |bibcode = 2006SSRv..125..331H | issue=1–4| s2cid = 32825899 | url = http://centaur.reading.ac.uk/190/1/ISSI2005_final.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Haigh | first1 = J. D. | title = The effects of solar variability on the Earth's climate | doi = 10.1098/rsta.2002.1111 | journal = Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 361 | issue = 1802 | pages = 95–111| year = 2003 |bibcode = 2003RSPTA.361...95H | s2cid = 53007804 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Haigh | first1 = J. D. | title = CLIMATE: Climate Variability and the Influence of the Sun | doi = 10.1126/science.1067013 | journal = Science | volume = 294 | issue = 5549 | pages = 2109–2111 | year = 2001 | pmid =  11739941| s2cid = 955158 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Haigh | first1 = J. D. | last2 = Pyle | first2 = J. A. | doi = 10.1038/279222a0 | title = A two-dimensional calculation including atmospheric carbon dioxide and stratospheric ozone | journal = Nature | volume = 279 | issue = 5710 | pages = 222 | year = 1979 |bibcode = 1979Natur.279..222H | s2cid = 4244566 }}</ref> She has served as editor of the ''Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences'' and a lead author on the [[Third Assessment Report]] of the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipcc.ch/ipccreports/tar/wg1/index.php?idp=558|title=IPCC - Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|website=ipcc.ch}}</ref> 

===Views on climate change===

Haigh conforms to the [[scientific opinion on climate change|mainstream scientific view]], that [[greenhouse gas|anthropogenic carbon emissions]] lead to increased [[greenhouse effect|greenhouse warming]]. She stated in June 2016 that if current levels of [[carbon dioxide]] emissions continued unabated, they would lead to a 5&nbsp;°C increase over [[temperature record|pre-industrial climate]] by the end of the next century, and that achieving a zero temperature rise would require a complete cessation of carbon emissions.<ref name="iop">{{cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/news/16/jun/page_67498.html|title=Atmospheric physicist Joanna Haigh takes on climate change at the IOP|date=9 June 2016|access-date=21 January 2017|publisher=Institute of Physics}}</ref> She also stated that she was optimistic about the future, following the [[2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference|COP21 conference]],<ref name="iop"/> but later, when [[Donald Trump]] became president of the United States, she said: {{quote|"If Trump does what he said he'd do, and others follow suit, my gut feeling is that I'm scared. Very scared."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-38676898|title=World v Trump on global climate deal?|date=21 January 2017|access-date=21 January 2017|last=Harrabin|first=Roger|work=BBC News}}</ref>}}

===Awards and honours===
In the [[2013 New Year Honours]], Haigh was appointed a [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) "for services to physics".<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=60367 |date=29 December 2012 |page=8 |supp=y }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.cabinetoffice.gov.uk/sites/default/files/resources/NY2013-list.pdf | title = New Year Honours List 2013 – General List | publisher = Cabinet Office | access-date = 29 December 2012}}</ref> Haigh served as president of the [[Royal Meteorological Society]] from 2012 to 2014; she is now{{when|date=November 2020}} a vice-president.<ref name="rmets">{{cite web|title=President and Council – Royal Meteorological Society|url=http://www.rmets.org/about-us/people/president-and-council|access-date=14 October 2014}}</ref><ref name=tls /> In 2013, she was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS). Her nomination read:<ref name="FRS">{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/people/joanna-haigh|title=- Royal Society|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>

{{quote|text=Distinguished for her scientific leadership in the area of solar influences on the middle atmosphere and for her modelling of how these effects can modulate tropospheric circulations and so propagate to Earth's surface. Her expertise in modelling atmospheric [[radiative transfer]] allowed the development of computationally fast but accurate radiative transfer schemes some of which are now in use by [[climate model]]ling groups across the world. By proposing and demonstrating an entirely novel mechanism for solar influence on climate she has allowed proper allowance to be made for the small and subtle, yet revealing effects.}}

In 2004 she received the [[The Chree Medal and Prize|Charles Chree Medal and Prize]] from the [[Institute of Physics]] and in 2010 the Royal Meteorological Society Adrian Gill prize for her work on solar variability and its effects on climate.<ref>{{cite web|title=Joanna Dorothy Haigh – Royal Meteorological Society|url=http://www.rmets.org/about-us/people/joanna-dorothy-haigh|access-date=14 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141018105918/http://www.rmets.org/about-us/people/joanna-dorothy-haigh|archive-date=18 October 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In November 2020 she was included in the [[BBC Radio 4]] [[Woman's Hour]] Power list 2020.<ref name="WomansHour_2020PowerList">{{cite web |title=Woman's Hour Power List 2020: The List |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/5f6X3JsVjcGXfXstdbYxhkk/womans-hour-power-list-2020-the-list |website=BBC Radio4 |access-date=16 November 2020}}</ref> She was interviewed by [[Jim Al-Khalili]] for ''[[The Life Scientific]]'' in 2013.<ref name=tls/>

Haigh is a [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics]] (FInstP).<ref name=whoswho/>
